title: Occasion of the poem
short: Bradstreet addresses her book, The Tenth Muse (London, 1650), published without her knowledge; the poem was written when a revised second edition was being prepared.
body: Bradstreet's brother-in-law, the Rev. John Woodbridge, took her manuscript poems to England, where they were printed in 1650 as The Tenth Muse Lately Sprung Up in America, the first book of poems by a woman resident in English America. The poem, written around 1666, when a second edition was under consideration, was printed in the posthumous second edition, Several Poems (Boston, 1678). The extended conceit of the book as an unruly child, which the author tries to clean and dress, runs throughout. The self-deprecation is a long-standing humility convention, but it also has personal force for a woman writing for print in Puritan New England.

title: The book as child
short: The governing conceit: the book is Bradstreet's child, born of her brain, which she must now clean, dress and send into the world.
body: Books as children of their authors' minds is an old figure (Plato's Symposium speaks of poems as children of the soul; Sidney calls Arcadia his 'child'). Bradstreet makes it maternal and domestic: the infant 'after birth' stays by its mother, is washed, dressed, and finally sent out 'of door'. The 'feeble brain' is a conventional apology, but as a woman's apology it engages the period's assumptions about female intellect, which Bradstreet elsewhere challenges in her 'Prologue'.

title: The unauthorised publication
short: Refers to Woodbridge's taking her manuscripts to London; the friends were loyal ('true') but unwise. 'Then' means 'than'.
body: The line pays the friends a backhanded compliment: they meant well but showed poor judgement. 'Then' was a common seventeenth-century spelling of 'than', used again in l. 16 ('more hobling then is meet'). Woodbridge's preface to The Tenth Muse indeed claimed he printed the poems without the author's knowledge. Bradstreet later wrote to her publisher in terms that suggest she knew of the plan, so whether she was truly surprised has been questioned; the claim of unwilling publication was a familiar modesty device, especially for women authors, so the poem may be partly conventional.

title: 'in raggs, halting to th' press'
short: The book went to press dressed in rags and limping; 'halting' means lame. ('Mae', as printed in the archive, is a misprint for 'Made'.)
body: The archive's 'Mae' reproduces a typographical slip for 'Made'; standard texts read 'Made thee in rags'. The rags are the faults of the first edition (errors in transcription and printing that Bradstreet regrets in the next line), and 'halting' (limping) anticipates the metrical joke on feet in l. 15. 'Trudg' means to walk wearily, and 'all may judg' is ironic: anyone can see the errors were not corrected in the press.

title: The 'rambling brat'
short: Her embarrassment that the unkempt child, now 'in print', publicly claims her as mother.
body: 'Brat' could mean simply a child, often with a contemptuous edge, and 'rambling' suggests both a wandering child and diffuse, disordered writing. The parenthesis '(in print)' points to the public exposure: what was private is now displayed. Her 'blushing was not small' (l. 7) suggests both a mother's shame at a child's behaviour and a woman's modesty at public attention.

title: visage, irksome
short: Its face was so annoying to her that she cast it aside, a mother's rejection quickly overcome by affection.
body: 'Visage' means face, and 'irksome' means tiresome or disagreeable. The mother's first impulse is to reject the child 'as one unfit for light' (that is, for public view), but natural affection ('being mine own') makes her try to improve it instead. The lines dramatise an author's ambivalence towards her published work. The phrase 'unfit for light' plays on the idea of a deformed infant hidden from the world, and on the publication of a book, which brings it to light.

title: Washing the child's face
short: Revision is like washing a child: each attempt to remove a blemish creates another, a wry comment on the endlessness of correction.
body: The domestic image describes Bradstreet's own revisions for the second edition, which were substantial. The witty observation that correcting one fault introduces another is familiar to any reviser. Critics often single out these lines as evidence of Bradstreet's humour and her confident use of domestic experience as poetic material. 'Still' means 'always' or 'each time', a common seventeenth-century sense, so the failure is presented as inevitable rather than occasional.

title: Metrical feet
short: A pun: she stretches the child's limbs to make its feet even, as she revises her lines to make the metrical feet regular.
body: The pun on 'feet' (body and metre) is the poem's sharpest wit. The book's verses still 'run ... more hobling then is meet', that is, limp more than is fitting; 'meet' means proper. The poem itself is written in regular heroic couplets (rhymed iambic pentameter), so the complaint of hobbling verse is partly a modest disclaimer. Stretching joints may also recall the rack, giving the image of revision a touch of violence.

title: 'home-spun Cloth'
short: She has nothing finer to dress the book in than plain homespun, an image of modest style and colonial domesticity.
body: Homespun cloth was woven at home rather than bought, and in New England it suggested frugality and self-reliance. The image claims a plain style for her verse, consistent with Puritan suspicion of ornament, and implies the material modesty of a colony far from London's fashions. It also echoes the classical convention of the book sent out in plain dress, found in Ovid's Tristia 1.1, where the exiled poet's book goes to Rome unadorned.

title: 'Vulgars' and 'Criticks'
short: She allows the book to go among ordinary readers but warns it away from critics.
body: 'Vulgars' means the common people (Latin vulgus, crowd), here unpretentious readers. The warning against critics reflects the risks for a woman poet whose work might be judged by learned men; in her 'Prologue' Bradstreet had anticipated readers who would say her hand was better suited to a needle. The address to one's book as it is sent into the world has classical precedents in Horace (Epistles 1.20) and Ovid (Tristia 1.1).

title: 'If for thy Father askt'
short: The book is to say it has no father, so it seems illegitimate: a joke about female authorship and the absence of a male author or patron.
body: The ending extends the conceit to its limit. A child without a father was a bastard, and the line plays on the scandal of a book without a male author or sponsor. Some critics read 'Father' as her husband or her own father, Thomas Dudley, both public men in Massachusetts, whom she will not implicate; others as a male literary model (Bradstreet had admired Du Bartas and Sidney), whose paternity she disclaims. Feminist readers find here an assertion of the book as wholly hers.

anchor: to send thee out of door
title: Sending the child out
short: The poor mother sends the child out to make its own way, ending on the image of the book as an orphan of necessity.
body: Poor families in the period often sent children out to service or apprenticeship; the mother's poverty 'caus'd her thus to send thee out of door'. The closing couplet combines humility (she is 'poor' in talent) and resignation, and it makes publication an act of letting go. The poem frames Bradstreet's second edition with the ambivalence of an author who corrects, disowns and finally releases her work.
